cards.front: Isotretinoin: why is it restricted in women of reproductive age?
cards.back: It is highly teratogenic. Up to about a quarter of exposed fetuses have birth defects, mainly craniofacial, cardiac and CNS abnormalities. It is contraindicated in women who may become pregnant during treatment and for one month after stopping.

cards.front: Isotretinoin: where is it used and what is the usual course?
cards.back: Oral 13-cis retinoic acid for severe cystic acne that has not responded to other treatment. The usual dose is 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily for about 20 weeks, and relapses can be treated by repeating the course. Half-life is about 18 hours, and unlike acitretin it does not accumulate in fat.

cards.front: Acitretin: indications and its pregnancy and alcohol precautions.
cards.back: Oral synthetic retinoid for severe psoriasis, lichen planus and severe ichthyosis. It is highly teratogenic and accumulates in body fat, so elimination takes months. Avoid conception during treatment and for 3 years after stopping, and avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 months after.

cards.front: Benzoyl peroxide in acne: how does it act and what are its limits?
cards.back: In the presence of water it releases oxygen, which kills P. acnes and other anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria. It also has keratolytic and comedolytic action, and bacteria do not develop resistance. It causes irritation and dryness, bleaches hair and fabric, and must not be applied together with tretinoin because it breaks the tretinoin down.

cards.front: Calcipotriol: mechanism and place in psoriasis.
cards.back: A synthetic vitamin D analogue that has little systemic effect on calcium when used topically. It binds the vitamin D receptor in keratinocytes, reducing proliferation and promoting differentiation. Response takes 4 to 8 weeks, efficacy is comparable to a moderate-potency steroid, and combining it with a steroid works better than either alone.

cards.front: Keratolytics: salicylic acid and urea, concentrations and uses.
cards.back: Salicylic acid at 10 to 20% (in alcohol or propylene glycol) dissolves corns and works better under an occlusive dressing; 3 to 5% is used in other conditions. Urea at 5 to 20% acts as a humectant that softens keratin in ichthyosis and hyperkeratotic lesions, and it enhances penetration of a topical steroid applied with it.

cards.front: Short note: Isotretinoin in acne vulgaris

points: Reduces sebum output and corrects abnormal follicular keratinisation
Bacterial numbers fall secondarily
Severe cystic acne that has not responded to other therapy
About 20 weeks at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily
Cheilitis, dry skin, eyes, nose and mouth, epistaxis
Raised serum lipids, raised intracranial pressure, musculoskeletal pain
Highly teratogenic; contraindicated in women who may conceive during therapy
Also avoid pregnancy for one month after stopping

cards.front: Short note: Drugs for psoriasis

points: Corticosteroids: start high potency, then step down; occlusion speeds response
Calcipotriol (vitamin D analogue) and tazarotene (retinoid prodrug)
PUVA: oral methoxsalen, then UVA exposure 1 to 2 hours later
Risks include skin cancer, cataract and premature skin ageing
Oral acitretin; PUVA for severe disease
Methotrexate weekly for moderate-to-severe psoriasis (avoid with liver disease; watch interacting drugs); cyclosporine microemulsion (monitor BP and creatinine)
Apremilast, an oral PDE4 inhibitor
Biologics: TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), IL-17 blockers (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-12/23 blocker ustekinumab, IL-23 blockers (guselkumab, risankizumab)
Controls lesions but does not cure; relapse is common on stopping

cards.front: Essay: Acne vulgaris: pathogenesis and drug management

points: Androgen-driven sebum excess in follicles
P. acnes colonisation; bacterial lipases release irritant free fatty acids
Comedones form and may rupture into inflammation and pustules
Benzoyl peroxide: antibacterial and comedolytic; bacteria do not become resistant
Retinoids: tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene; benzoyl peroxide inactivates tretinoin, so do not apply together
Topical antibiotics (clindamycin, erythromycin) for inflamed papules, combined with benzoyl peroxide to improve efficacy and limit resistance; azelaic acid
For extensive acne or acne not controlled by topical therapy
Oral tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) or macrolides
Isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne, with strict teratogenicity precautions
Tretinoin: start at a low strength; response takes 6 to 10 weeks
Long-term tetracyclines can cause raised intracranial pressure

cards.front: Classify: sunscreens and sun protection
cards.text: Chemical sunscreens such as {{PABA}} absorb UVB, {{benzophenones}} block UVA, and physical sunscreens such as {{zinc oxide}} and {{titanium dioxide}} scatter UV and visible light. SPF is the UVB dose causing minimal erythema on protected skin divided by the dose on unprotected skin.

cards.front: Classify: topical corticosteroid potency (KDT grading)
cards.text: Potent: {{clobetasol propionate}}, betamethasone valerate and fluocinolone acetonide 0.025%; moderately potent: {{mometasone}} and fluticasone; mild: {{hydrocortisone}}. Potency depends largely on the {{lipophilicity}} of the compound, which governs how deeply it penetrates the skin.

cards.front: Complete: demelanising agents
cards.text: {{Hydroquinone}} is a weak agent that inhibits {{tyrosinase}} and needs months of use in melasma; {{monobenzone}} destroys melanocytes and can cause {{permanent depigmentation}}.

cards.front: Define disinfection and sterilisation, and state the difference.
cards.back: Sterilisation kills all microbes, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogenic microbes to a level that does not endanger a person with normal defences, so it does not necessarily kill everything. Antiseptics are used on living tissue and disinfectants on inanimate objects.

cards.front: Hexachlorophene: why was its use restricted?
cards.back: A chlorinated phenol that is odourless, non-staining and persists on skin, but it is narrow spectrum: it kills gram-positive bacteria, not gram-negative bacteria or spores. A 3% bath for infants cut staphylococcal infection but caused brain damage in premature neonates, and preparations above 2% have been banned.

cards.front: Chlorhexidine: class, mechanism and main uses.
cards.back: A cationic biguanide that disrupts bacterial membranes and denatures proteins. It is more active against gram-positive bacteria and persists on skin. Used for surgical scrub, neonatal bath, obstetric and general skin antisepsis, and as a 0.12 to 0.2% mouthwash for gingivitis; repeated use can stain teeth brown.

cards.front: Ethanol as an antiseptic: effective concentration and limits.
cards.back: Effective at 40 to 90%, fastest near 70%, because it precipitates bacterial proteins. It does not kill spores and promotes rusting of instruments. It irritates mucosa, the scrotum and open wounds, where it forms a coagulum that can shelter bacteria. Alcohol-based rubs are used for hand hygiene.

cards.front: Povidone-iodine: what is it, and how does it differ from tincture iodine?
cards.back: An iodophore: iodine bound to polyvinylpyrrolidone that releases free iodine slowly. It is non-irritant, non-staining and long-acting, and it does not blister when covered with a dressing. Tincture iodine (2% in alcohol) stings on abrasions. Povidone-iodine is used on boils, burns, ulcers, tinea, vaginitis, surgical scrubs and endoscope disinfection.

cards.front: Permethrin: why is it the first-choice drug for scabies?
cards.back: A pyrethroid that paralyses the insect nervous system. Human toxicity is very low, systemic absorption is minimal and resistance is rare. A single application cures most scabies and lice, including cases that did not respond to lindane. For scabies, 5% cream is applied over the body except face and scalp and washed off after 8 to 12 hours.

cards.front: Short note: Lindane

points: Broad-spectrum insecticide that enters the chitinous cover and affects the nervous system
Effective against lice and scabies after one treatment
Lice: applied to scalp for 12 to 24 hours; repeat after one week if needed
Scabies: applied below the neck, scrub bath 12 to 24 hours later
Lipid soluble, so absorbed through skin, especially from oily vehicles and in children
Resistance reported; less effective than permethrin
CNS stimulation, convulsions and cardiac arrhythmias
Avoid in infants, young children and pregnancy

cards.front: Short note: Ivermectin in scabies and lice

points: Anthelmintic that is also effective against ectoparasites
The only oral drug used for ectoparasitosis; used less often because good topicals exist
Single oral dose of 0.2 mg/kg (about 12 mg in adults)
Cures roughly 91 to 100% of scabies cases, including patients with AIDS
Not for children under 5 years, pregnant women or breastfeeding women
Very few side effects

cards.front: Essay: Scabies: drugs and control

points: Contagious mite infestation that burrows through the epidermis and causes intense itch
Finger webs are the usual entry site; spreads to forearms, trunk, genitals and legs
Permethrin 5% cream: single application, first choice
Benzyl benzoate: second-line; contraindicated in children due to neurological effects
Lindane: effective but systemic toxicity risk; avoid in children and pregnancy
Crotamiton: lower cure rate; a 5-day course is used in children
Sulfur: cheap but messy and malodorous; largely superseded
Oral ivermectin when topical drugs are unsuitable
Treat family contacts together; wash garments and bed linen in hot water

cards.front: Classify: scabicides and pediculicides
cards.text: First choice: {{permethrin}}; second line: {{benzyl benzoate}} and {{crotamiton}}; older agents: {{sulfur}} and {{DDT}}; oral option: {{ivermectin}}.

cards.front: Classify: oxidising agents, aldehydes and halogens
cards.text: {{Potassium permanganate}} and {{hydrogen peroxide}} are oxidising agents; {{glutaraldehyde}} is less irritant than {{formalin}}, which is a 37% solution of {{formaldehyde}}.

cards.front: Complete: silver compounds
cards.text: {{Silver nitrate}} 1% is used for {{ophthalmia neonatorum}} because it is highly active against {{gonococci}}; {{silver sulfadiazine}} is used on burns because it is highly active against {{Pseudomonas}}.

cards.front: What features make a chelating agent clinically useful?
cards.back: It must form a stable ring with the metal, ideally a 5 to 7 membered ring with two or more ligand groups. It should bind the toxic metal more strongly than calcium and the body's own ligands, distribute into the same compartments as the metal, and be water soluble. Its efficacy falls as the gap between exposure and treatment increases.

cards.front: Dimercaprol: which metals does it treat, and what is the main contraindication?
cards.back: It treats arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning, and is an adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning. It is contraindicated in iron and cadmium poisoning, because its complexes with these metals are themselves toxic.

cards.front: Calcium disodium EDTA: main use, route and key toxicity.
cards.back: Given intravenously because it is not absorbed orally and does not enter the brain. It is the mainstay for lead poisoning and also treats iron, zinc, copper, manganese and some radioactive metals, but not mercury. Its main toxicity is proximal tubular necrosis, which is reduced by keeping urine flow high.

cards.front: Disodium EDTA: why must it be infused slowly?
cards.back: It is a potent calcium chelator, so rapid intravenous injection causes tetany. A slow infusion avoids this because calcium is drawn from bone. For emergency hypercalcaemia bisphosphonates are preferred.

cards.front: Penicillamine: which isomer is used, and what are its main indications?
cards.back: The D-isomer, because the L-isomer and the racemate cause optic neuritis. Indications are Wilson's disease (0.5 to 1 g daily, taken 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals), copper or mercury poisoning, cystinuria and cystine stones, and scleroderma. Prolonged use causes skin, renal, haematological and collagen toxicity.

cards.front: Desferrioxamine: what is it used for and what is its chelating capacity?
cards.back: An iron chelator derived from an actinomycete. One gram binds about 85 mg of elemental iron. It removes loosely bound iron and iron from ferritin and haemosiderin, but not iron in haemoglobin or cytochromes. Used in acute iron poisoning (mainly children) and transfusion siderosis; it is given parenterally because little is absorbed orally.

cards.front: Short note: Dimercaprol (BAL)

points: Oily compound developed as an antidote to the arsenical war gas lewisite
Two SH groups bind metals that inactivate sulfhydryl enzymes; 2:1 complexes are most stable
Arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning
Adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning
Intramuscular 5 mg/kg stat, then 2 to 3 mg/kg every 4 to 8 hours for 2 days
Then once or twice daily for 10 days; start early and alkalinise urine
Dose-related rise in BP, tachycardia, vomiting, burning, sweating and headache
An antihistamine given 30 minutes before reduces the reactions

cards.front: Short note: Iron chelators

points: Acute iron poisoning, mainly in children
Transfusion siderosis in thalassaemia and other chronic iron overload
Parenteral; histamine release causes flushing, hypotension and urticaria
Repeated use can cause lens and retinal changes
Oral; somewhat less effective than desferrioxamine but cheaper and more convenient
Anorexia, vomiting, joint pain and reversible neutropenia; agranulocytosis rare
Oral once daily on an empty stomach; iron complex excreted in bile
High affinity for iron, low for copper and zinc; GI bleeding and renal failure reported

cards.front: Essay: Chelation therapy in heavy metal poisoning

points: Chelators form stable ring complexes that the body excretes
Early treatment matters: efficacy falls as the delay increases
Ideal agent: high affinity for the toxic metal, water soluble, matching distribution
Arsenic and mercury: dimercaprol or succimer; penicillamine as an alternative for mercury
Lead: calcium disodium EDTA, with succimer preferred for chronic lead
Copper: penicillamine; iron: desferrioxamine, deferiprone or deferasirox
Dimercaprol intramuscular; calcium EDTA intravenous only; succimer and deferasirox oral
Calcium EDTA stays extracellular and does not reach the brain
Dimercaprol: dose-related hypertension and pain; antihistamine pre-treatment helps
Calcium EDTA: proximal tubular necrosis and febrile reactions
Penicillamine: skin, renal and haematological toxicity on long-term use

cards.front: Classify: chelators by target metal
cards.text: Dimercaprol and {{succimer}} treat arsenic and mercury; {{calcium disodium edetate}} treats lead; {{penicillamine}} treats copper in Wilson's disease; {{desferrioxamine}} treats iron overload.

cards.front: Complete: adverse effects of chelators
cards.text: Rapid intravenous {{disodium edetate}} causes {{tetany}} by chelating calcium; {{calcium disodium edetate}} can cause {{proximal tubular necrosis}}, which is reduced by high {{urine flow}}.

cards.front: Complete: oral iron chelators
cards.text: {{Deferiprone}} is an oral option that can cause reversible {{neutropenia}}; {{deferasirox}} is given once daily on an empty stomach and is excreted in {{bile}}.

cards.front: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins: how do they differ in storage and toxicity?
cards.back: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored for long periods, so regular large doses can accumulate to toxic levels. Water-soluble vitamins (B complex and C) are poorly stored and excess is excreted, so toxicity is rare. Water-soluble vitamins mostly act as cofactors for enzymes.

cards.front: Vitamin A: features of deficiency.
cards.back: Xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, corneal softening (keratomalacia) and night blindness progressing to total blindness. Also dry rough skin with follicular papules, increased infection, diarrhoea, urinary stone formation, impaired spermatogenesis and growth retardation. Common in infants and children in developing countries.

cards.front: Vitamin A: chronic and acute toxicity.
cards.back: Chronic: about 100,000 IU daily for months causes nausea, dermatitis, hair loss, bone pain, raised intracranial pressure and liver disease; it is also teratogenic, so daily intake should stay under about 20,000 IU. Acute: over 1 million IU gives headache, drowsiness, vomiting and skin shedding; treat by stopping intake and giving vitamin E. Excess carotenoids do not cause toxicity.

cards.front: Vitamin E: why is antioxidant use for heart disease and cancer not justified?
cards.back: Large observational studies and meta-analyses have not shown fewer cardiovascular events or cancers in well-nourished people, and high doses (over 400 mg/day of tocopherol) have been linked to heart failure. No clear human deficiency syndrome exists. Its recognised uses are narrow: supplementation for at-risk patients, G6PD deficiency and acanthocytosis.

cards.front: Isoniazid and vitamin B6: what is the interaction and how is it handled?
cards.back: Isoniazid combines with pyridoxal and increases renal loss of pyridoxine, which can cause deficiency and peripheral neuropathy. Pyridoxine at 10 to 100 mg/day prevents or treats these effects and is routinely given with anti-MDR-TB regimens. Hydralazine, cycloserine and penicillamine also interfere with pyridoxine.

cards.front: Pellagra: classic features and which niacin form is preferred for treatment?
cards.back: The three Ds: dermatitis (a sunburn-like rash that darkens and peels), diarrhoea with glossitis and stomatitis, and dementia. Treatment is 200 to 500 mg/day in divided doses. Nicotinamide is preferred, especially by injection, because nicotinic acid causes flushing and other side effects.

cards.front: Short note: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency

points: Converted to thiamine pyrophosphate, a coenzyme in decarboxylation and the hexose monophosphate shunt
Requirement rises with carbohydrate intake (about 0.3 mg per 1000 kcal)
Mainly polyneuritis: numbness, weakness, wrist drop or foot drop
Mental changes, poor memory and constipation
Cardiovascular: palpitation, high-output heart failure and ECG changes
Oedema from heart failure, worsened by protein deficiency
Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis: high-dose parenteral thiamine (about 100 mg/day)
Beriberi: 100 mg/day intramuscular or intravenous, then oral maintenance; prophylaxis 2 to 10 mg/day

cards.front: Short note: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

points: Needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen
Also needed for carnitine, catecholamine and steroid synthesis, and for folate conversion
Scurvy: capillary fragility, bleeding gums, petechiae, brittle bones, poor wound healing
Seen in malnourished infants, the elderly, alcoholics and drug users
Scurvy: 0.5 to 1.5 g/day; prevention 50 to 100 mg/day
Improves iron absorption; acidifies urine in urinary tract infection
Rebound scurvy after stopping long-term mega-doses
Urinary oxalate stones; cytotoxic if added to iron preparations

cards.front: Essay: Vitamins: rational use, deficiency and toxicity

points: Organic, non-energy-yielding compounds needed in small amounts
Main drug role is preventing and treating deficiency
Poor intake, malabsorption, raised need, increased loss, genetic defects and drug interactions
Stored in the body, so toxicity is cumulative
Vitamin A: teratogenic; keep daily intake under about 20,000 IU
Generally low toxicity; excess is excreted
Pyridoxine: sensory neuropathy at 0.2 to 2 g/day; ascorbic acid: rebound scurvy
Vitamins are over-prescribed; many popular claims lack evidence
Antioxidant supplements have no proven benefit in well-nourished people

cards.front: Classify: vitamins and their coenzyme forms
cards.text: Thiamine forms {{thiamine pyrophosphate}}; riboflavin forms {{FAD}} and {{FMN}}; niacin forms {{NAD}} and {{NADP}}; pyridoxine forms {{pyridoxal phosphate}}.

cards.front: Classify: signs of vitamin deficiency
cards.text: Scurvy reflects a {{connective tissue}} defect; {{angular stomatitis}} and corneal vascularisation point to riboflavin deficiency; {{seborrhoeic dermatitis}} and glossitis suggest pyridoxine deficiency.

cards.front: Fill: vitamin C and iron
cards.text: Vitamin C improves {{iron}} absorption by keeping it in the {{ferrous}} state; abrupt stopping of large doses can cause {{rebound scurvy}}.

cards.front: Active versus passive immunity: which products give each, and which gives immediate protection?
cards.back: Vaccines give active immunity by stimulating the recipient's own antibody or cell-mediated response, which takes weeks. Antisera and immunoglobulins give passive immunity with ready-made antibodies, so protection is immediate but short-lived. Only antisera are also curative for an established infection.

cards.front: Live attenuated vaccines: who must not receive them?
cards.back: People with impaired defences: leukaemia or other malignancy on cytotoxic chemotherapy, systemic lupus, those on corticosteroids, and those with AIDS or other immunodeficiency. Two live vaccines not given together should be separated by about one month. Vaccines are also deferred during pregnancy and acute infection.

cards.front: Sabin (OPV) versus Salk (IPV) polio vaccine: which is preferred for children and for adults?
cards.back: OPV (live, Sabin) is the vaccine of choice for children in KDT: easy to give, it induces intestinal as well as systemic immunity and limits carriage, which is the basis of pulse polio campaigns. It is shed in stool, so it can spread to contacts, and rarely (about 1 per million doses) causes vaccine-associated paralysis; the USA stopped using it in 2000. IPV (inactivated, Salk) mainly induces humoral immunity, does not spread or cause paralysis, and is preferred for adults, immunocompromised people (OPV is contraindicated in primary immunodeficiency), pregnant women and children with symptomatic HIV.

cards.front: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: intradermal (Thai) regimen and intramuscular schedule.
cards.back: KDT (Thai regimen, notified in India in 2006): 0.1 ml of PCEV or PVRV, or 0.2 ml of HDCV, intradermally at two sites on days 0, 3 and 7, then one site on day 28 and one on day 90; about one-fifth of the i.m. vaccine dose. GG14 (i.m.): four doses on days 0, 3, 7 and 14, with rabies immunoglobulin on day 0, part infiltrated into the bite and the rest i.m. RIG is needed for category III bites because the vaccine takes 10 to 14 days to produce antibodies. A previously vaccinated person needs only two doses (days 0 and 3) and no RIG.

cards.front: Human versus equine antisera: which is preferred for rabies and tetanus?
cards.back: Human immunoglobulin is preferred. Human rabies immunoglobulin (20 IU/kg on day 0, infiltrated around the bite) and human tetanus immunoglobulin (250 to 500 IU prophylaxis) have longer half-lives and rare serum sickness. Equine rabies serum (40 IU/kg) and tetanus antitoxin (1500 to 3000 IU) are used only when the human product is unavailable.

cards.front: Polyvalent antisnake venom: which venoms does it neutralise, and how is it given?
cards.back: Each ml neutralises standard venom of Indian cobra, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper and common krait. Give 20 ml intravenously at about 1 ml/min, repeated every 1 to 6 hours until signs of envenomation stop. Viper bites may need up to about 300 ml; some serum is also infiltrated around the bite to limit local gangrene.

cards.front: Short note: Typhoid vaccines

points: S. typhi plus S. paratyphi A and B; 0.5 ml subcutaneously in 2 to 3 doses
About 70% effective for one year; more local and systemic reactions
Single 0.5 ml dose; about 72% protection at 18 months
Fewer reactions; no paratyphoid protection; not for children under 2 years or in pregnancy
Attenuated strain lacking Vi; enteric-coated capsules on alternate days (3 doses in KDT; GG14 describes a 4-dose course)
Protection for about 3 years; not for young children or in pregnancy
Vi and Ty21a give better and longer protection with fewer adverse effects than TAB

cards.front: Short note: Hypersensitivity and serum sickness with antisera

points: Urticaria, angioedema, respiratory distress and anaphylaxis
Keep adrenaline 1:1000 ready and ask about any past reaction to serum
Intradermal or scratch test before equine serum
A positive test contraindicates use; a negative test does not rule out systemic sensitivity
Serum sickness 7 to 12 days later: fever, rash, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy
More common with large or repeated doses; overall about 5 to 10%
Arthus-type local reaction after intramuscular injection
Human immunoglobulins do not cause serum sickness

cards.front: Essay: Vaccines: types, examples and contraindications

points: Killed or inactivated: organism inactivated by heat or chemicals; several doses, shorter immunity
Live attenuated: avirulent but still replicates; usually long-lasting immunity
Toxoids: detoxified exotoxins that keep their antigenicity
Killed: cholera, pertussis, influenza, inactivated polio, hepatitis A, rabies (HDCV, PCEV)
Live: BCG, oral polio, MMR, varicella, oral Ty21a typhoid
Toxoid or subunit: tetanus, diphtheria, Vi polysaccharide, recombinant hepatitis B
Defer during acute (especially respiratory) infection and pregnancy
Poor response during steroid or immunosuppressant therapy; keep adrenaline available
Live vaccines in immunocompromised people; MMR and varicella in pregnancy
Pertussis: not after a severe reaction or with a history of convulsions

cards.front: Classify: vaccines by type
cards.text: Killed vaccines include {{cholera}}, {{pertussis}} and {{influenza}}; live attenuated vaccines include {{BCG}}, {{MMR}} and {{varicella}}; toxoids include {{tetanus}} and {{diphtheria}}.

cards.front: Fill: hepatitis B vaccine
cards.text: The hepatitis B vaccine is a {{recombinant}} surface antigen made in {{yeast}} cells, given as three doses at {{0, 1 and 6}} months, with protective antibody in about 99% of recipients.

cards.front: Fill: passive immunity products
cards.text: Hepatitis B immune globulin should be given within {{7 days}} of exposure to HBsAg-positive blood; normal human gamma globulin is used for prophylaxis of {{hepatitis A}}, {{measles}} and {{chickenpox}}.

cards.front: Short note: Vitamin D

points: D3 (cholecalciferol) made in skin by UV light; D2 (ergocalciferol) from plant ergosterol
Liver forms 25-OH D3 (calcifediol), the main circulating form with the longest half-life
Kidney 1-hydroxylation to calcitriol is rate-limiting: stimulated by PTH, low calcium and low vitamin D; calcitriol inhibits it
Calcitriol raises intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption (calbindin)
Acts on bone to mobilise and mineralise; behaves like a hormone (made in body, nuclear receptor, feedback control)
Prophylaxis (400 IU/day) and treatment of nutritional rickets and osteomalacia
Vitamin D-dependent and renal rickets: calcitriol or alfacalcidol (no renal hydroxylation needed); vitamin D-resistant rickets: phosphate plus calcitriol
Hypoparathyroidism; with calcium in osteoporosis
Chronic high doses (about 50,000 IU/day) cause hypercalcaemia: weakness, vomiting, polyuria, renal stones, nephrocalcinosis, ectopic calcification
Treat by stopping the vitamin, low-calcium diet, fluids and corticosteroids

cards.front: Vitamin K: forms, mechanism, main uses, and why menadione is avoided.
cards.back: K1 (phytonadione, phytyl side chain) is from plants, K2 (menaquinones) is made by gut bacteria, and K3 (menadione) is synthetic. It is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X (also proteins C and S), letting them bind calcium. Uses: deficiency from diet, antibiotics or obstructive jaundice; haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (1 mg i.m. at birth); and, most important, overdose of oral anticoagulants, for which K1 is preferred because it acts fastest (avoid unnecessarily high doses, which cause warfarin resistance for days). I.v. emulsified K1 can cause severe anaphylactoid reactions. Menadione causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and neonates and can precipitate kernicterus.

cards.front: Vitamin B12: causes of deficiency, features and treatment.
cards.back: Causes: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor), other gastric damage or gastrectomy, intestinal malabsorption or resection, blind-loop bacteria or fish tapeworm, and (less often) a strict vegetarian diet. Features: megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, glossitis, and neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuritis). Treatment is by injection when intrinsic factor is lacking; hydroxocobalamin is preferred because it is more protein-bound and better retained (e.g. 1 mg i.m. daily or alternate days for 2 weeks, then every 1 to 3 months). Add folic acid and iron, because brisk haemopoiesis can unmask their deficiency. Neurological recovery is slow and may be incomplete.

cards.front: Folic acid: uses, and why it must never be given alone in vitamin B12 deficiency.
cards.back: Uses: megaloblastic anaemia from poor intake, malabsorption, pregnancy and other high-demand states, and antiepileptic therapy (avoid large doses, which can weaken anticonvulsant control); therapeutic dose 2 to 5 mg/day orally. Routine supplementation in pregnancy reduces neural tube defects. Given alone in B12 deficiency it corrects the blood picture but the neurological damage worsens, because the small B12 store is diverted to haemopoiesis. Folinic acid (already reduced) is reserved for methotrexate toxicity; it is not needed for simple folate deficiency.

cards.front: Short note: Disinfectants and antiseptics: classes and mechanisms

points: Phenol (carbolic acid): disrupts bacterial membranes and denatures proteins; standard for comparing germicides
Cresol and chloroxylenol: more active and less tissue-damaging than phenol
Hexachlorophene: inhibits bacterial enzymes and causes lysis at high concentration
Iodine and iodophores (povidone-iodine): iodinate and oxidise microbial protoplasm
Chlorine and chlorophores (chlorinated lime, sodium hypochlorite): release hypochlorous acid
Chlorhexidine: cationic; disrupts the bacterial membrane and denatures proteins
Quaternary ammonium compounds (cetrimide, benzalkonium chloride, dequalinium): alter membrane permeability and denature proteins
Pseudomonas, mycobacteria and spores resist cationic agents
Ethanol and isopropanol: precipitate bacterial proteins; effective at 40 to 90 percent ethanol
Formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde: denature proteins; glutaraldehyde is a better sterilant when activated
Potassium permanganate: liberates oxygen that oxidises protoplasm

cards.front: Short note: Corticosteroids in dermatology

points: Anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, vasoconstrictor and antiproliferative effects
Potency depends mainly on lipophilicity: fluorinated and lipid-soluble esters are the most potent
Penetration is highest at axilla, groin, face, scalp and scrotum; lowest on palms, soles, elbows and knees
Milder preparations for atopic eczema and allergic contact dermatitis; potent ones for alopecia areata, discoid lupus, lichen planus, keloids and psoriasis of palms and soles
Use the mildest effective preparation; potent ones only briefly or intermittently
Occlusion can raise absorption many-fold; continuous occlusion encourages infection
Absorption is higher in infants and children
Twice-daily application is enough; more applications add no benefit
Local: skin thinning, striae, telangiectasia and easy bruising, related to potency and duration
Systemic: adrenal suppression with large amounts used repeatedly, especially in children; rarely Cushing's syndrome

cards.front: Short note: Antiseptics - selectivity

points: Most antiseptic-disinfectants act widely (non-selective)
Hexachlorophene, chlorhexidine, quaternary ammonium compounds, gentian violet and acriflavine are more active against Gram-positive than Gram-negative organisms
